questions.q: Which split supports the 95.2% headline, and what is reported for unseen speakers?
questions.answer: The 95.2% sentence-level word accuracy is on the overlapped-speaker split (255 random test sentences per speaker). On held-out speakers 1, 2, 20, and 22, the paper reports 88.6% accuracy and Table 2 gives 6.4% CER / 11.4% WER.

questions.q: Is the comparison with the previous GRID state of the art a like-for-like benchmark?
questions.answer: No. The cited 86.4% Gergen result is speaker-dependent isolated-word accuracy, while LipNet's headline is sentence-level accuracy on an overlapped-speaker split; Table 1 does not supply the prior test partition or decoder details. The conclusion's 2.8× comparison therefore needs its task and metric conversion stated explicitly.

questions.q: How were human lipreaders tested, and which model comparison is directly reported?
questions.answer: Three hearing-impaired participants learned the GRID grammar, viewed 10 minutes of annotated training videos, and labelled 300 random evaluation videos. On the unseen-speaker split their mean was 47.7% WER; LipNet was 11.4% WER. The paper gives 1.69× higher accuracy in the introduction, 4.2× lower WER in Sec. 4.3, and 4.1× better performance in the conclusion.

questions.q: How much does the language model affect the reported results?
questions.answer: The no-LM ablation has 13.6% vs 11.4% WER on unseen speakers and 5.6% vs 4.8% on overlapped speakers; the authors summarise the increase as approximately 1.2×.

questions.q: Which evaluation details needed for exact replication are absent?
questions.answer: The paper does not report training seeds or repetitions, a separate validation/checkpoint-selection protocol, session-level partitioning, the random seed or selected items for the overlap test subset, or a chance-level baseline. It reports LipNet's training-set RGB normalisation and beam/LM settings, but does not itemize decoder/LM settings for every baseline.

questions.q: What limitations do the authors themselves acknowledge?
questions.answer: GRID's fixed grammar and restricted position-specific vocabulary help contextual prediction; the authors defer larger-data and joint audio-visual evaluations to future work, and report that most residual errors fall within visually confusable viseme groups.

questions.q: Writer-run reader questions (free-model reader runs on arxiv-1601.08188, w2594690981-lrw, isca-gergen16-streamw, arxiv-1611.05358, aaai-38133-linprovsr and the target were started but had not returned within the time box; the writer therefore opened only the specific passages named in the loc fields of entries w1-w4, c1-c4, g1-g4, l1-l5, s1-s4, q1-q5 and verified every quote with verify_quotes.py).
questions.answer: Gergen et al.'s 86.40% is a video-only accuracy from speaker-dependent word HMMs decoded with the full GRID task grammar and reported on a 5% development subset, so the target's 2.8x comparison crosses task level, split and decoder constraint. Wand et al. classify single words cut with corpus alignments and report a cross-speaker standard deviation and a t-test. Chung and Zisserman found 3D convolutions about 14% worse than 2D ones for word classification. Watch, Attend and Spell (concurrent, Nov 2016) reaches 3.0% GRID WER with an attention decoder under the target's own 255-utterance protocol. The best GRID WER in the wiki today is 0.99% (LinProVSR, AAAI 2026), still with a 3D convolution front end.
